blocks.text: I hear that the female of the turtledove, once widowed of her mate, restrains herself out of longing for her spouse and admits no other mate into her nest. Chrysostom, Homily [II, 555] On the Turtledove, English edition, vol. 7, p. 264: Φασί τινες τὴν τρυγόνα φίλανδρον εἶναι, καὶ φίλαγνον· ὥς τε κἂν συμβῇ τὸν ταύτης ἄῤῥενα ὑπὸ ἀετοῦ ἀναλωθῆναι, ἢ ὑπὸ ἰξευτοῦ θηρευθῆναι, ταύτην ἑτέρῳ ἀνδρὶ μὴ ἐπιμίγνυσθαι, ἀλλ᾽ αὐτὸν ποθεῖν, αὐτὸν ἀναμένειν, καὶ τῇ τούτου μνήμῃ συναποθνήσκειν. [Phasi tines tēn trygona philandron einai, kai philagnon; hōs te kan symbē ton tautēs arrena hypo aetou analōthēnai, ē hypo ixeutou thēreuthēnai, tautēn heterō andri mē epimignysthai, all᾽ auton pothein, auton anamenein, kai tē toutou mnēmē synapothnēskein.] Some say that the female turtledove is held by love for her mate and is so devoted to chastity that, if her male happens to be taken by an eagle or by a fowler, she does not mate with another, but longs for and awaits him alone, and even dies together with the memory of him. So also Gregory of Nyssa, Homily 3 on the Song; Epiphanius in the Physiologus, ch. 10; Philo of Carpasia on Cant. 1.; Ambrose in the Hexaemeron, book 5, ch. 19, and on Psalm. CXVIII.; Jerome, Against Jovinian, book 1, ch. 17; Justus of Urgel, [col. 24] Theodoret, Aponius and Gregory the Great on Cant. I, 10.; Eustathius on the Hexaemeron; Ildefonsus of Toledo, Sermon on the Purification of St Mary, if it is really his; Theophylact on Luke, ch. 2; Pisides, On the Creation of the World, line 998; Geoffrey, Abbot of Vendôme, Sermon 7; Michael Glycas, Annals, section 1; Bernard on the Song, Sermons 40 and 59, and the Sermon on the Nativity of St Mary, On the Aqueduct; the Baal Hatturim on Levit. XII, 6.; R. Selomo on Psalm. LXXIV, 19.; Damir in the chapter On شفنين [shifnīn] siphnin, that is, the turtledove. All these, I say, attribute to the turtledove what the older writers had written of the dove alone: that she is so devoted to one mate that, when he dies, she does not admit another. As a result, those who have commented on the Song of Solomon have not sufficiently understood why Solomon so often designates the bride by the name of his dove. Thus Cant. II, 14.: My dove, in the clefts of the rock, etc. And Cant. V, 2.: Open to me, my sister, my love, my dove. And Cant. VI, 8.: My dove, my perfect one, is but one, etc. By this, clearly, he wished to signify that she was loved by him alone, and that he in turn was uniquely dear to her, just as among doves there is a remarkable love between mates and a very firm law of marriage. If this was less true in the type, that is, in Solomon, who had wives by the ἑκατοντάδας [hekatontadas], it is nevertheless most true ἐν τῷ τυπωθέντι [en tō typōthenti], that is, in Christ: just as we acknowledge him alone as bridegroom, so he has one church, which he has betrothed to himself for ever in righteousness, judgment, lovingkindness and mercy, Os. II, 19. Hence the Apostle, 2 Cor. XI, 2.: I have espoused you to one husband, that I may present you as a chaste virgin to Christ.

Although המה properly means to make a noise and to be in tumult, nevertheless the Hebrew מעי המו in Cant. V, 4. the Greeks render ἡ κοιλία μου ἐθροήθη [hē koilia mou ethroēthē], and Jerome, My belly trembled. So too in Ezech. VII, 16., where the same Jerome has, They shall be on the mountains like doves, all trembling, and Junius, They shall be on the mountains themselves like doves of the valleys, all trembling: the words all trembling correspond to the Hebrew כלם המות. And in Os. XI, 11., for ויחרדו you may read in Junius, they shall come running in trepidation, etc., like a dove from the land of Assyria. In others: they shall tremble, or they shall fear, or they tremble like a dove, etc. These expressions exactly capture the dove's nature. For the dove [II, 556] is a most fearful animal. Hence Varro on doves, On Agriculture, book 3, ch. 7: Because of their natural fear they seek the highest places on roofs. And a little later: For nothing is more timid than a dove. And in Ovid, Metam. book 5, Fable 10, the nymph Arethusa says of herself and of Alpheus pursuing her:
So I ran, so that wild one pressed upon me, As the dove flees the hawk on trembling wing, And as the hawk is wont to harry trembling doves.
The dove, once wounded by your talons, hawk, [col. 24] is terrified by the slightest whirring of a wing.
And Valerius Flaccus, in the eighth book of the Argonautica, of Medea:

But lo! the maiden, after the manner of a frightened dove, When, encompassed by the huge shadow of a bird of prey, She falls trembling upon whatever man she meets. Just so she, Struck with heavy fear, threw herself into the midst, etc.
As the Chorus in Sophocles' Ajax, line 139:

— — — πεφόβημαι
Πτηνῆς ὡς ὄμμα πελειάς. [pephobēmai / Ptēnēs hōs omma peleias.]
I fear, like the eye of the winged dove. And another poet in the Suda, under Πελειάδες [Peleiades]:
Δειλαί τοι δείλοισιν ἐφεδρεύουσι πέλειαι, [Deilai toi deiloisin ephedreuousi peleiai,]
